newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends with light LME gains, aluminium firm.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends with light LME gains, aluminium firm.

text.p: Copper prices backtracked from earlier highs during Monday afternoon LME trading, but still closed steadier, against a background of June tightness ahead of Wednesday's option declarations.
Elsewhere, aluminium firmed up and raced up towards the $1,600 level during the latter part of the session, but other contracts were mixed.
Copper prices trended higher from the outset, as July/threes and cash/threes widened out to near $170 backwardation.

However, there was some lending interest throughout the rest of the session, while the market also stalled near $2,440 resistance. By the close, three months was back at $2,422, up just $4 from Friday's kerb, while the cash/threes rate was around $145.
Aluminium found the impetus to chase up and challenge the resistance stretching up to $1,600, building on the supportive buying seen on recent dips.
Although the close was just under $1,600, the charts are in better shape, and further gains should be secured if the run of stock draw-downs continues. Last trade was at $1,598, up $23 from Friday.
Nickel prices held above early 6-1/2 month lows during the afternoon, but still closed lower after confirming technical weakness under $7,000 today.
The rally from the lows reflected news that a weekend explosion at Outokumpu's Harjavalta smelter would result in 5,000 tonnes of lost production. Copper output was only briefly interrupted.
This helped the nickel market partially recover from the hit taken after the ending of a four week strike at Inco Sudbury. Last trade was at $6,860, still down $110.
Zinc continued to correct lower after earlier failing to break above a 6-3/4 year high around $1,430, and prices closed at $1,418, down $10.
The market was hit by expected technical selling, a slight widening in the contango to around $5, and an LME stock increase of a net 1,875 tonnes, with 2,750 tonnes delivered into Singapore.
There has been talk of quality problems with some Chinese zinc, which may be why recent talk of sizeable tonnages being delivered into Singapore has not evidenced itself in the data.
However, there may be significant tonnages off-warrant, and Chinese exports this year will be substantially above 1996 levels, analysts noted.
Lead was lacklustre throughout, and closed at $627, down $3 from Friday. Tin was equally lifeless, and ended at $5,570, up just $10. Alloy was stable at $1,450/60 a tonne.
